chunks: Bed-of-nails test fixtures. The question: What are bed-of-nails test fixtures? What can they capture?
A bed-of-nails fixture is a custom holder packed with spring-loaded pins, called pogo pins, placed to match the test pads on one specific board.
The board is pulled down onto the pins, so every pin touches its pad at once. The pins are wired to a tester that can measure any part of the board.
It tests hundreds of connections in seconds.
Think of the pin-art toy: lots of loose pins that press against an object and take its shape. The fixture is a stiff version.
Each pin is a small spring, so it keeps pushing gently even if some pads are a bit lower than others.
All those springs add up to a large force, so the board must be supported and pulled down firmly. Unlike the toy, every pin has a wire and a job.
Side view. Spring probes (blue) stand in the probe plate; the board is pulled down so each tip lands on a test pad (orange) on the underside.
The probes' rear ends are wired to the tester. Atmospheric pressure acting on the board over the evacuated cavity (red arrows), or a clamshell lid, supplies the force.
Pogo pin: a spring-loaded probe with a plunger, spring and barrel. Test pad: an exposed copper spot, usually at least about 0. 9 mm across, where a pin lands.
Probe plate: the drilled plate that holds each pin at its board coordinates. Vacuum fixture: one that sucks air out under the board so air pressure pushes it onto the pins.
Registration: aligning the board to the pins, using precise holes in the board (tooling holes) that fit over guide pins.
Say each pin presses with about 100 g of force, and the fixture has 1,500 pins.
The total is 1,500 x 100 g = 150 kg of force on the board, so vacuum or a press must hold it firmly. Alignment errors from the holes, drilling and pin wobble might add up to ±0.
15 mm. A 0. 9 mm pad has a 0. 45 mm radius, so the pin still lands on the pad with margin. That is the whole idea.
"A bed-of-nails fixture is a custom plate of spring-loaded pogo pins positioned to match the test pads on one board.
A vacuum or clamshell presses the board onto all the probes at once, and the tester measures through them.
It captures shorts, opens, component values and polarity for ICT, and powered and functional behaviour for FCT, in seconds.
The costs are the fixture, test pads and layout constraints, mechanical force and alignment, and probe wear that causes false fails."
